analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting health benefits already promised to retirees, and orders cut benefits restored.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing: referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced in September 2002 with no cosponsors, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal law governing employer health plans (ERISA) to stop companies from canceling or reducing health benefits after an employee has retired — including cuts hidden in higher copays, dropped coverage, or forced moves into managed care. It would also require companies to restore benefits they had already taken away from current retirees, unless they could prove doing so would cause substantial business hardship, with a federal loan-guarantee program (capped at $5 billion) to help struggling companies finance the restoration. Companies with fewer than 100 people covered would be exempt, and retirees could waive their own protections in writing or through collective bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees of employer health plans who counted on lifetime health coverage and then saw it cut or canceled after they retired. The bill's own findings describe retirees who, because of preexisting medical conditions, could not buy replacement coverage without draining their life savings, and some who saw their health deteriorate after being shifted into inadequately managed plans. Once retired, these people generally cannot go back to work or re-enter the insurance market on fair terms, so locking in the benefits they were promised matters most to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees whose promised health coverage was cut

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans from making any post-retirement reduction in retiree health benefits, overriding plan language that reserves a general right to amend or terminate, and treats terminating a plan as a violation if retirees don't keep the same benefits.

Requires plans to offer current retirees restoration of benefits that were cut after their retirement date, with written notice itemizing what must be restored and its value, and a restoration window opening within a year of enactment.

Creates an enforceable regime: the Labor Secretary may assess civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation for each affected participant or beneficiary, and existing ERISA enforcement provisions apply.

Waivers are available only on a showing of substantial business hardship, and are barred outright for companies that could have moved excess pension assets into a retiree health account but didn't, or that ran a well-funded pension plan while skipping retiree cost-of-living adjustments — targeting firms with money to pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor retiree health plans, which would have to keep paying benefits they promised and, for plans covering 100 or more people, retroactively restore benefits already cut. Taxpayers bear contingent exposure through the loan-guarantee program — up to $5 billion in outstanding guarantees, a $200 million program cost appropriation, and $10 million for administration, all designated as emergency spending.

drawbacks.text: The retroactive restoration mandate lands on companies all at once. A firm hit with years of restored benefits could respond by cutting jobs, freezing wages, or dropping coverage for current workers and pre-retirees — costs the bill doesn't compensate; the hardship waiver is the only safety valve, and firms that fail the waiver test might instead cut benefits for workers who haven't retired yet, since the bill only protects people after their retirement date.

The loan-guarantee program creates federal financial exposure: up to $5 billion in outstanding guarantees and $210 million in appropriations designated as emergency spending, backstopping loans to companies that private lenders would not finance on reasonable terms — precisely the companies most likely to default.

The protection is narrow in scope: it exempts plans covering fewer than 100 participants, applies only to benefits in place the day before retirement, and lets retirees waive their rights in writing or through collective bargaining — so a worker whose benefits were cut just before retiring, or whose union agreed to concessions, is not covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise-keeping rule — no cutting retiree benefits after retirement — addresses a real and widely documented harm to people with no practical way to replace lost coverage, and the waiver process, small-plan exemption, and consent provisions give it reasonable escape valves. The heaviest and least-cushioned cost is the retroactive restoration requirement, which falls entirely on employers and could strain weak companies; the loan guarantees partially offset that but add federal exposure. On balance a defensible bill for a vulnerable group, with the main honest objection being its abrupt retroactive reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the bill on September 5, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.

The bill's findings state that retirees of ERISA-regulated plans had been severely harmed by the 'virtually unchecked' practice of sponsors canceling or reducing health benefits after retirement, causing a crisis in retiree health care.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or brought to a vote.
Sponsor Paul Wellstone died in a plane crash on October 25, 2002, seven weeks after introducing the bill, leaving it without its Senate champion for the session's final months.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that sponsor retiree health plans came out ahead: they kept the existing legal freedom to trim, restructure, or cancel retiree health benefits without new federal penalties, and no restoration obligation was imposed. Retirees who lost benefits got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping control of retiree benefits

for.name: Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Retiree Health Benefits Protection Act and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor joined, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded; the bill's only action was a same-day committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would bar these companies from cutting retiree health benefits after retirement and force larger ones to restore benefits already taken away, unless they prove substantial business hardship. Their interest in continuing to trim these promised benefits runs directly against the retirees who counted on them.

A new federal program would guarantee their loans — up to $5 billion outstanding — to companies financing benefit restoration, with fees paid to Treasury. The banks' interest runs alongside the public purpose here, since the guarantees exist to help sponsors pay retirees what they owe.

Plans would have to embed an explicit no-post-retirement-cuts clause in their contracts and forgo flexibility to restructure retiree coverage, but most would keep administering the plans either way; the main pressure falls on the sponsoring employers.
